scenes.heading: Equations with Fractions
scenes.subheading: Grade 9 Mathematics · Factorisation and equations, part 4
scenes.narration: Welcome to part four of our Grade 9 series on factorisation and equations. In this lesson we solve equations with fractions, including fractions with x in the denominator.

scenes.heading: The method
bullets: Find the LCD of all the denominators
Multiply every term on both sides by the LCD
If $x$ is in a denominator, write down what $x$ cannot be
scenes.narration: Here is the method. Find the lowest common denominator of all the fractions. Multiply every term, on both sides, by the LCD, and the fractions disappear. And if x is in a denominator, first write down the values x cannot be, because we can never divide by zero.

scenes.heading: Example 1
scenes.narration: Solve x minus one over three, minus x plus two over four, equals one. The LCD is twelve. Multiply every term by twelve, keeping the tops in brackets: four times, x minus one, minus three times, x plus two, equals twelve. Expand: four x minus four, minus three x, minus six, equals twelve. So x minus ten equals twelve, and x equals twenty two.

scenes.heading: Example 2
scenes.narration: Solve two x over five, plus x over two, equals nine. The LCD is ten. Ten times two x over five is four x. Ten times x over two is five x. Ten times nine is ninety. So nine x equals ninety, and x equals ten.

scenes.heading: Example 3: x in the denominator
scenes.narration: Solve three over x, plus one half, equals two. x is in a denominator, so x cannot be zero. The LCD is two x. Multiply every term by two x: six, plus x, equals four x. Subtract x: six equals three x. So x equals two, which is allowed.

scenes.heading: Example 4: A fraction on each side
scenes.narration: Solve four over x plus one, equals two over x minus one. The denominators cannot be zero, so x cannot be negative one, and x cannot be one. Multiply both sides by both denominators, or cross multiply: four times, x minus one, equals two times, x plus one. Expand: four x minus four equals two x plus two. So two x equals six, and x equals three.

scenes.heading: Check your answer
scenes.narration: Let us check x equals three. The left side is four over four, which is one. The right side is two over two, which is also one. Both sides are equal, so x equals three is correct.

scenes.heading: Tips
bullets: Multiply every term by the LCD, even whole numbers
Keep a top with two terms in brackets
Reject any answer that makes a denominator zero
scenes.narration: Three tips. Multiply every term by the LCD, even the whole numbers. Keep a top with two terms in brackets, so the signs come out right. And reject any answer that would make a denominator zero.
